title: A compacted topic still shows old records for a key you thought was deleted — why (tombstone retention)?
shortTitle: A compacted topic still shows old records for a key you thought was deleted — why (tombstone retention)?

s1_definition.profdef: In a compacted topic, deleting a key means producing a tombstone, which is a record with the key you want to delete and a null value. Log compaction eventually removes all earlier records for that key and keeps the tombstone as the proof of deletion. But compaction is asynchronous and partition-local: it only runs on the dirty, non-active portion of the log, it does not touch the active segment, and the tombstone itself is kept around for at least `delete.retention.ms` so that every consumer has a chance to observe the delete. So if you read right after writing a tombstone, you can still see old records for that key because the cleaner has not yet processed that part of the log.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India keeps one noticeboard per account where only the latest notice should remain. To cancel Rajesh's standing instruction, a clerk pins a special blank "cancelled" slip with his account number on it. But the noticeboard tidy-up happens on a schedule, and the clerk doing the tidy-up never touches the slips pinned in the last few minutes, and the rule also says to leave the blank cancelled slip up for a full day so every branch reads it before it is removed. So if you glance at the board moments after pinning the cancelled slip, Rajesh's old instruction is still visible. It is not a bug; the cleanup simply has not reached that part of the board yet.
s1_definition.oneliner: Deletion in a compacted topic is a tombstone, and compaction is a lazy background job that skips the active segment and keeps tombstones for `delete.retention.ms`, so seeing old records for a "deleted" key right after the delete is expected timing, not a failure.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** In a compacted topic, deleting a key means producing a tombstone, which is a record with the key you want to delete and a null value. Log compaction eventually removes all earlier records for that key and keeps the tombstone as the proof of deletion. But compaction is asynchronous and partition-local: it only runs on the dirty, non-active portion of the log, it does not touch the active segment, and the tombstone itself is kept around for at least `delete.retention.ms` so that every consumer has a chance to observe the delete. So if you read right after writing a tombstone, you can still see old records for that key because the cleaner has not yet processed that part of the log.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India keeps one noticeboard per account where only the latest notice should remain. To cancel Rajesh's standing instruction, a clerk pins a special blank "cancelled" slip with his account number on it. But the noticeboard tidy-up happens on a schedule, and the clerk doing the tidy-up never touches the slips pinned in the last few minutes, and the rule also says to leave the blank cancelled slip up for a full day so every branch reads it before it is removed. So if you glance at the board moments after pinning the cancelled slip, Rajesh's old instruction is still visible. It is not a bug; the cleanup simply has not reached that part of the board yet.

**One line to remember:** Deletion in a compacted topic is a tombstone, and compaction is a lazy background job that skips the active segment and keeps tombstones for `delete.retention.ms`, so seeing old records for a "deleted" key right after the delete is expected timing, not a failure.

sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India keeps a compacted topic `account.profiles` that holds the latest profile snapshot per account, so services can rebuild an account cache by replaying the topic. Rajesh is SAV2001 and Priya is CUR3001.

Problem 1 — compliance asked us to delete Rajesh's profile from the stream. We produced a tombstone for SAV2001, then immediately replayed the topic to verify, and were alarmed to still see three old SAV2001 profile versions. This is exactly the compaction-lag problem: the cleaner had not yet processed the segments holding those old versions, and they were ahead of the tombstone in the log.

Problem 2 — a downstream cache service replayed the topic but ignored null values, so even after compaction it kept a stale SAV2001 entry. This is the consumer-side half of the problem: a tombstone only works if the consumer treats a null value as a delete instruction.

Our runnable demo models a `CompactedLog` with segment files, a `LogCleaner` that compacts only closed segments and honors tombstone retention, and a `ProfileCacheConsumer` that correctly applies tombstones. We write several versions of SAV2001, then a tombstone, read before and after a cleaning pass, and show the consumer's view with and without null handling. The classes are `TombstoneDemo`, `CompactedLog`, `LogSegment`, `LogCleaner`, and `ProfileCacheConsumer`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three versions of SAV2001's profile and one CUR3001 profile in a first segment, then a tombstone for SAV2001 in the active segment.

Step 1: The producer appends profile-v1, profile-v2, a CUR3001 profile, and profile-v3 for SAV2001. These land in the first segment, which then rolls closed, so a new active segment begins.

Step 2: Compliance deletes SAV2001 by producing a record with key SAV2001 and a null value. This tombstone lands in the active segment.

Step 3: A verification read immediately after sees everything, including the three old SAV2001 versions, because the log cleaner has not yet run and it would never touch the active segment anyway. This is the moment people mistake for a bug.

Step 4: The log cleaner runs a compaction pass over the closed segments. It keeps only the latest record per key among closed segments and rewrites them. The three old SAV2001 versions collapse, but the tombstone itself stays in the active segment and is retained for delete.retention.ms so slow consumers still see the delete.

Step 5: A consumer that handles tombstones replays the log, applies the null value as a delete, and ends with no SAV2001 entry in its cache. A buggy consumer that ignores null values keeps a stale SAV2001 entry forever, which demonstrates that correct tombstone handling is a shared responsibility between the topic and the consumer.

Final output:

```

  │  ProfileCacheConsumer         │

  │ + apply(Record):              │
  │     value==null -> remove     │  (correct)
  │     value!=null -> put        │
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Key Lifecycle in Compacted Log ──────────────────

  [LIVE v1..vN] ──tombstone (null)──→ [MARKED_DELETED]
        │                                   │ cleaner pass: drop old values
        │                                   ▼
        │                           [ONLY_TOMBSTONE]
        │                                   │ after delete.retention.ms + next pass

  2. read immediately -> old versions still visible (cleaner not run)

  5. consumer.apply(null) -> cache.remove("SAV2001")
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
In a compacted topic, deleting a key does not remove a row the way a database delete does. Instead you publish a tombstone, which is a record carrying the key with a null value. Compaction then promises to keep at least the latest value per key and, over time, to remove the older values and eventually the tombstone itself. The reason you can still see old records for a key you thought you deleted is that compaction is a lazy, asynchronous background job with several timing rules, so what you are seeing is almost always expected timing rather than a failure.

There are three timing rules that cause this. First, compaction runs in the background via the log cleaner, so there is always a gap between your write and the physical removal of old values. Second, the cleaner only works on closed segments, never on the active segment that is still being appended to, and it only bothers once the stale fraction of the log crosses the cleanable dirty ratio, so recent records simply have not become eligible yet. Third, the tombstone is deliberately retained for the delete retention window, which defaults to twenty-four hours, so that consumers that are behind get a chance to actually read the delete before it vanishes. Until a cleaning pass has processed the segments holding the old values, those old values sit ahead of the tombstone in the log and are perfectly visible.

On the National Bank of India profile stream we hit this exactly. Compliance asked us to delete Rajesh's profile from the compacted account.profiles topic. We produced a tombstone for his account, immediately replayed the topic to verify, and still saw three old versions. Nothing was wrong: the cleaner had not yet run on the closed segments and would never have touched the fresh tombstone in the active segment. After a compaction pass the old versions collapsed, and the tombstone stayed for the retention window so our slower consumers could still learn about the delete.

The second half of the lesson is that tombstones only work if consumers cooperate. One of our cache services was ignoring null values, so even after compaction it kept a stale entry for Rajesh forever. The fix was to make every consumer treat a null value as an instruction to evict the key from its local view. When I need deletes to take effect faster, I tune the topic by rolling segments sooner, lowering the cleanable dirty ratio so the cleaner runs more aggressively, and shortening the delete retention window, but I never set that window so short that a slow consumer could miss the delete and hold a stale key. The one thing I always warn about is that a record with a null key cannot be compacted at all, because compaction is keyed, so a mistakenly null-keyed record will linger until ordinary retention removes it.

---

keyPoints: Retention: time-based (7 days default) or size-based
Compaction: keep latest value per key — delete old versions
Compacted topic: acts as a key-value snapshot store
